title: Sticky egress IP granularity and DNS caching playbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This playbook documents a proposed design and Terraform module notes for implementing sticky/allocated egress IPs and an on-prem DNS caching/forwarding layer for Private deployments (VPC/on-prem). It focuses on operational guarantees: preserving client source IP stability (important for customer allowlists, external partner ACLs), reducing DNS latency and egress DNS lookups, and providing predictable NAT/failover behavior during upgrades.

Scope and constraints:
- Applies to Private deployments (VPC and fully on-prem clusters) where tenants or logical services require stable outbound IP addresses.
- Target environments: k8s (kubeadm/RKE/managed on-prem distributions), BGP-enabled edge routers, NAT appliances or Linux-based NAT hosts, and local DNS caching nodes.
- Goal: minimize host-level iptables hacks; prefer deterministic allocation with observable mapping and easy rollback.
- Not covered: multi-cloud cross-region BGP peering, direct internet proxying for compliance review (separate doc).

High-level design summary:
1) Egress model: sticky egress IPs allocated at a granular scope (service / namespace / tenant). Allocation levels supported: single-pod SNAT (for strict isolation), namespace-scoped IP pool (good balance), and cluster-shared IPs (default). Allocation is controlled by a Terraform-managed IPPool CRD + controller that programs SNAT rules on egress nodes.
2) NAT HA: NAT implemented with two options (fallthrough):
   - Preferred: dedicated NAT hosts (Linux) with keepalived (VRRP) + BGP advertisement of floating IPs to edge routers. This provides fast failover and on-prem parity with cloud-managed NAT.
   - Alternative: kube-proxy-based SNAT per-node with external HA router NAT (less stable for per-tenant sticky IPs).
3) DNS layer: local caching/forwarder tier (dnsmasq/unbound) per-AZ/room. Split-horizon resolution for private hostnames. Upstreams: internal authoritative resolvers -> optional external resolvers. Use EDNS for performance and DNSSEC validation where required.
4) Firewall and egress policies: coarse-grained L3 firewall rules at the rack/edge, k8s NetworkPolicies for pod-level enforcement, and an egress-proxy (optional) at the service level for HTTP(s) inspection and allowlisting.

Terraform module notes (sketch):
Modules envisioned (each as its own module in terraform-modules/private-networking):
- ip_pool: manages IP pools for sticky allocation. Exposes variables: pool_name, cidr, allocation_scope (pod|namespace|cluster), reserved_ips, tags. Creates CRD manifest (IPPool) applied with k8s provider.
- nat_gateway: provisions NAT host(s) (compute instance or baremetal VM) + keepalived config + BGP peering resources (if using FRR on on-prem routers). Variables: nat_count, flavors, failover_mode (vrrp|bgp), asn, bgp_neighbors. Outputs: floating_ips[], nat_hosts[].
- dns_forwarder: deploys DaemonSet/Deployment for dnsmasq or unbound, configmaps for forwarders, and CoreDNS patch to forward cluster lookups. Variables: forwarders[], cache_ttl, stub_domains (map), healthcheck_path.
- firewall_rules: fabric-level rules, modeled as a list of rule blocks: name, source, dest, ports, proto, action, environment. Can emit cloud provider firewall resources or on-prem static configs.
- network_policy_templates: curated set of k8s NetworkPolicies for common patterns (service-egress-only, db-access-only, allow-dns-to-cache).

Important implementation details and decisions:
- Sticky mapping persistence: mapping table stored in a k8s CRD (EgressMapping) with TTL and manual overrides. Controller watches assignment requests and programs NAT hosts via an agent (gRPC API) that updates nftables rules. This avoids ephemeral iptables rules scattered across nodes.
- Granularity tradeoffs: pod-scoped IPs yield strongest isolation but require more floating IPs and NAT host capacity; namespace-scoped IPs are often sufficient for SaaS customers who want an allowlist per-customer.
- IP exhaustion: ip_pool module must include an autoscaling alert and a fallback behavior (picked by policy): 1) auto-fallback to shared pool, 2) queue requests causing 429s, or 3) error and require manual action.
- Healthchecks & failover: NAT hosts export metrics (peer_state, conntrack_entries, active_mappings). keepalived + BGP sessions must be monitored; automations to reprovision on unhealthy nodes included in nat_gateway module.

Kubernetes interactions and network policies:
- EgressMapping CRD links to a ServiceAccount or Namespace annotation to request allocation. Example annotation: network.redwood.ai/egress-pool: "tenant-42-namespace-pool"
- Controller will add an iptables/nftables SNAT rule on the node where traffic exits, matching selector by node egress gateway pods. Consider leveraging eBPF (Cilium) for more efficient rewriting in future.
- NetworkPolicy templates include explicit allow for DNS cache: 
  - allow UDP/53/TCP/53 from pods to dns-cache namespace
  - allow egress-proxy namespace to external endpoints

DNS caching/forwarding specifics:
- Each AZ/room runs 2 dns-cache replicas behind a local VIP (keepalived). Use dnsmasq for very low-latency cache and unbound when DNSSEC and validation is required.
- Split-horizon: CoreDNS configured with stubDomains map to route private.company.internal to internal resolvers. External lookups go to trusted public resolvers but rate-limited.
- Long TTLs for stable external endpoints, but respect service-registered low TTLs for dynamic services. Provide a config toggle to override TTLs for cache warming during upgrades.

Upgrade and rollout plan (high level):
Phase 0: Prep and dry-run
  - Create test cluster that mirrors production NAT + DNS topology (small scale)
  - Apply ip_pool & dns_forwarder modules in test; validate allocation logic and mapping visibility
  - Create synthetic workloads that simulate source-ip sensitive traffic and DNS load

Phase 1: Pilot (canary)
  - Pick single non-critical customer namespace or internal service.
  - Allocate namespace-scoped egress IP from new pool and route its traffic via NAT hosts.
  - Monitor for connectivity, external partner allowlist acceptance, and connection quality for 72 hours.

Phase 2: Gradual expansion
  - Incrementally onboard more namespaces. Use Terraform workspaces or per-namespace configuration with the ip_pool module.
  - Introduce the dns_forwarder across AZs; switch subset of nodes to use local VIP for DNS and observe latency / NXDOMAIN rates.

Phase 3: Cluster-wide rollout & hardening
  - Migrate critical customer namespaces. Enable alerts for conntrack thresholds, NAT host CPU/memory, DNS cache miss rates, and BGP/VRRP flaps.
  - Run chaos scenarios: NAT host failover (simulated powerdown), BGP neighbor restart, DNS forwarder restart. Validate rollback plan.

Rollback steps (if severe regression):
- Remove annotations that assign sticky IPs for newly onboarded namespaces to force fallback to shared pool.
- Revert Terraform changes using apply on previous state (careful: preserve EgressMapping CRD state backup).
- Failover NAT VIPs to previous hosts if routing instability observed.

Observability & tests to add:
- Metrics: per-pool egress byte rates, active mappings, conntrack saturation, dns_cache_hit_ratio, dns_latency_p50/p95/p99.
- Logs: NAT host connection summaries, EgressMapping controller audit logs, CoreDNS/dnsmasq query logs (sampled).
- Synthetic tests: nightly egress-IP verification (external service records source IP), DNS lookup distribution test, BGP session flapping simulation in staging.

Runbooks and incident playbooks (short):
1) External partner reports allowed IP not matching:
  - Check EgressMapping CRD for customer namespace -> expected_ip
  - SSH to NAT host owning that floating IP -> check conntrack & SNAT rules
  - If NAT host is unhealthy, promote next host via keepalived and re-run conntrack cleanup script

2) High DNS latency / cache misses:
  - Verify dns-cache replicas health, CoreDNS forwarding config, and network MTU issues between pods and dns-cache VIP
  - Temporarily increase cache_ttl to reduce upstream lookups during mitigation

3) NAT host conntrack exhaustion:
  - Rate-limit new connections at edge, add more NAT hosts, clear stale conntrack entries with safe heuristics

Open questions / TODOs:
- Controller agent design: REST vs gRPC vs direct CRD reconciliation. Tradeoffs: auditability vs timeliness.
- eBPF path: prototype using Cilium for transparent SNAT and lower CPU than kernel iptables.
- Billing/usage accounting: how to attribute egress cost per customer if sticky IPs are used? Need a schema.
- Terraform state strategy: per-environment vs per-tenant. Recommend per-environment with locks for now.

Appendix - Quick TF variable examples (notes):
module "ip_pool_tenant42" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//private-networking/ip_pool"
  pool_name = "tenant-42-pool"
  cidr = "10.40.200.0/27"
  allocation_scope = "namespace"
  reserved_ips = ["10.40.200.1"]
}

module "nat_gateway_eu_west" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//private-networking/nat_gateway"
  nat_count = 2
  failover_mode = "vrrp"
  asn = 64512
  bgp_neighbors = ["10.10.1.1", "10.10.1.2"]
}

module "dns_forwarder" {
  source = "git::ssh://git@github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules.git//private-networking/dns_forwarder"
  forwarders = ["10.10.2.5", "10.10.2.6"]
  cache_ttl = 300
  stub_domains = { "private.company.internal" = "10.10.3.10" }
}

- Primary owner: Aisha Patel (eng-private-deployments)
- Review meeting: propose Wed 2026-03-03 10:00 PT with network infra and SRE
- Immediate next tasks: prototype ip_pool CRD controller (POC), test keepalived+FRR BGP pairing in lab, and baseline DNS cache performance for 1M queries/day.

Notes to reviewers: this is intentionally a design + ops playbook draft. Looking for feedback on the control-plane vs data-plane split, any regulatory concerns with mapping IPs per-tenant, and preferred Terraform state scoping.
